lesson.title: Why Numbers Need a Story: An Introduction to Statistics
lesson.summary: This section introduces statistics as the science of collecting, organizing, analyzing, and interpreting data to answer questions and make decisions in the presence of uncertainty.
lesson.body:
Statistics is the science of collecting, organizing, analyzing, and interpreting data in order to answer questions and make decisions when the world is uncertain. Notice that word: uncertain. If every measurement came out exactly the same every time, we would not need statistics at all. We would just measure something once and know the truth forever. But real measurements vary. Two students who each shoot ten free throws will not make the same number of shots. Two batches of the same cookie recipe will not weigh exactly the same. Statistics exists because variability is a basic fact of the world, and we need reliable tools for describing it, learning from it, and making decisions in spite of it.

It helps to think of statistics as a four step process. First, you collect data by observing, measuring, or surveying. Second, you organize and summarize that data so a huge pile of numbers becomes something a human being can actually look at, such as a table, a graph, or a single summary number like an average. Third, you analyze the data, looking for patterns, comparing groups, or checking whether a pattern is more than just random noise. Fourth, you interpret the results in plain language and connect them back to the original question. Skipping any one of these steps is how people end up misusing data, either by collecting it carelessly or by drawing conclusions the data cannot actually support.

Statistics is traditionally split into two branches. Descriptive statistics is about summarizing and displaying the data you actually have in hand, using tools like averages, percentages, and charts. Inferential statistics goes a step further: it uses data from a smaller group to draw conclusions about a much larger group that was not fully measured. Both branches depend on the same underlying data, but they answer different kinds of questions. Descriptive statistics answers "what did we observe." Inferential statistics answers "what can we conclude beyond what we observed."

Here is a small worked example of descriptive statistics in action. Suppose a basketball player attempts 10 free throws in practice and makes 7 of them. The proportion made is calculated by dividing the number of successes by the number of attempts: 7 divided by 10 equals 0.70, or 70 percent. That single number, 70 percent, is a statistic, a number that summarizes something about the data. It is useful, but it also has limits. Ten shots is a small number of attempts, so if the player shot another 10 free throws the next day, the result might be 6 makes, or 9 makes, purely due to chance. A large part of learning statistics is learning how much to trust a number like 70 percent, and how that trust changes as the amount of data grows.

Every other idea in this course builds on this foundation. Before you can summarize or analyze anything, you need data to work with, which is the subject of the next section. From there, you will learn how to describe individual pieces of information as variables and observations, how to organize them into datasets, and eventually how to use a manageable sample to learn something true about an entire population. Statistics, in other words, is the toolbox. The rest of this course is about learning to use each tool correctly.
